blocks.1: Aerial photograph of the church from 1962, municipal photo archive.
blocks.2: On p. 222 of the book on stone crosses in Norway, Birkeli writes: “The assemblies' decisions to convert to Christianity in fact meant an almost automatic division of the country into parishes.” Christianity was, as mentioned, considered adopted at the Gulating in 997, and it is said that “Evindvig parish”, now Gulen parish, is one of the oldest parishes in the country. The parish was called Eivindvik right up until the name was changed by royal decree of 17 May 1890, from Eivindvik to Gulen.
blocks.3: A map from 1771 shows that the parish covered almost all of outer Sogn, namely old Gulen, Brekke, Lavik, nearly all of Solund and Bø parish in Hyllestad. I have also had this confirmed at the State Archives in Bergen. The church in Eivindvik is marked as the main church, with annex churches in the parishes of Brekke, Bøe, Lavik, Husøy and Solund. To the east the parish bordered on Vik parish on the south side of the Sognefjord and on Leikanger on the north side, and to the north on “Ytre Holmedal”. We do not know when this large union began, but it is said to be very old. Lavik and Bø were separated by royal decree of 18 December 1807. Brekke was transferred to Lavik by royal decree of 24 April 1858, and the last church union with Solund was dissolved by royal decree of 22 October 1887. Brekke parish is now once again part of Gulen parish, as a result of the municipal merger in 1964.
blocks.4: The oldest written record found so far of a church here is a medieval charter in Diplomatarium Norvegicum dated 14 June 1327. B.E. Bendiksen writes on p. 610: “In 1327 the papal collector Bernhard de Ortis appoints the parish priests in Hammer and Evindvik as agents to collect two years' income from vacant livings (annates) in Nordhordland and to render account for it in Bergen”.
blocks.5: Johan Litleskare, who has written about Haus church, says on page 13 of his book that in a letter of 1329 Lord Audfinn assesses the papal tithe on the churches (and priests) according to the church's “rank and wealth”. Haus church is there “placed together with Eivindvik and Fana and stands as no. 2 after the county church, which of course stands first.” On p. 32 Litleskare writes about how much Haus church paid in war tax to “the Danish war chest” in 1563, and he adds: “Only Hamre church and the church in Eivindvik pay more”.
blocks.6: Historians believe a church stood here long before 1327; the church site is probably among the very oldest in the country. What is written above would suggest that the church here was well known and established when, even before 1330, it was ranked as one of the most powerful churches in a larger district. It is mentioned in official records as a main church. In a power of attorney (kept in the church archive) dated 11 March 1814, an oath sworn in “Evindvig's main church” the same day is mentioned. In a letter from the Ministry of Church and Education dated 4 August 1900, concerning the building of a church at Mjømna, the church in Eivindvik is called “Gulen's main church”. It says that there are to be 15 services a year at Mjømna, as the Bishop of Bergen shall decide in more detail, “but in such a way that the service on the first day of the great festivals is always held in Gulen's main church”. The main churches were built by order of the king (the state) and enjoyed greater protection and rank than other churches. The punishment for breaking the peace in a main church was, for example, that the offender was declared an outlaw, whereas in the so-called “high-seat churches” it was settled with fines. It seems to me that the churches called main churches were also county churches. The Christian law in the Gulating law shows that there is one church in each county called the main church, which all the men of the county are obliged to maintain. In “Kulturhistorisk leksikon for nordisk middelalder”, published in 1960, p. 39, it says: “Originally there was one county church or main church in each county”. In “Historisk Tidsskrift, second series, sixth volume”, published in 1888, Taranger writes on pp. 343–44 that the Eidsivating law, chap. 32, requires the bishop to come once a year “to each third and sing mass there at the main church, which corresponds to the county church of the Borgarting law.” Note no. 2 on p. 344 shows that the “identity” between county church and main church “applies only in the Frostating law, Viken and for the oldest time also the Gulating law.”
blocks.7: Perhaps from this we may assume that the church here was from of old a county church and main church?
blocks.8: Since then I have seen that a letter of 21 April 2008 from the National Archives to the parish priest Jens Linde says: "It seems clear that the church in Eivindvik, that is, Gulen church, has had the status of a main church throughout the period covered by the archive material."
blocks.9: The term "main church" has now gone out of use; church law no longer distinguishes between different types of church.
blocks.10: Legend says that when St Olav gathered the people to build a church in Eivindvik, a chieftain lived in Virkesdal, a giant of a man, called Torstein. The king's summons came to him too. It was in the middle of haymaking, and Torstein was out mowing when he got the message from the king. He grew angry and swung so hard that the scythe cut great furrows in the ground. The furrows are visible “to this very day”. The field where he was mowing is still called “Torsteinslette”.
blocks.11: When the worst of his anger had passed, he went into the forest and cut down a big tree. He took the log with him to Eivindvik and swore that if this log was not used as a doorpost in the church, he would not strike another blow on Olav's church. The king gladly accepted the splendid log, which was hewn and set in place as a doorpost in the church.
blocks.12: Tradition connects this doorpost with a post carved with T.V. and the year 1600, which is said to have stood in the church that was pulled down to make room for the church that stands today.
blocks.13: It is also part of this legend that King Olav did not like Torstein having brought a horse's leg as provisions, which he ate from while he worked and would not give up. Torstein left everything King Olav told him about the White Christ to stand for what it was worth, but that he should not be allowed to eat his tasty horse's leg he could not understand.
blocks.14: The clairvoyant Anna Elisabeth Westerlund believed that the first church here came as early as the 11th century. It was a small, simply built wooden church with an earth floor and hardly any seats. The roof was also of wood, of brown, probably tarred boards. It was not a stave church, Westerlund said. The church was very cold; people stood inside wearing lots of clothes. It had a porch and a small octagonal altar rail. This first church was not well received by the people. They had difficulty accepting the new faith, and they destroyed the church. A new church was built, also of wood. In this one there was a form of heating, with glowing coals in iron pans. The church was looked after and improved; the earth floor was replaced with a wooden floor.
blocks.15: After the Reformation the church was altered. Later it fell more and more into decay and in the end was in poor condition. Westerlund “saw”, among other things, a leaking roof. Finally the church was pulled down and the church that stands today took its place. So far Westerlund's “vision”.
blocks.16: Could it be that the church Westerlund “saw” as church no. 2 here was patched up and rebuilt several times and was in fact, originally, the same one that stood here before the present one came in 1863?
blocks.18: There is a good deal of information about the church that stood here before the one we have now, and I have picked out some of it from copies from the archive of the Directorate for Cultural Heritage. My sources for the material on “the new church” are mostly E. Bjordø's book, together with the parish register for Gulen parish, earlier anniversary publications for the church and conversations with people in the village.
blocks.19: “The old church” is thought to have been built a little before 1600. From a house in Gulen that was renovated in 1993, I was given a piece of a post said to have stood in “the old church”. A good deal of material bought when the church was auctioned off in 1863 was used in this house. The owner of the house does not wish to be named or to say where the house is, but I have also heard from others that this house contains a lot of material from “the old church”.
blocks.20: The post has kept very well. It appears to have stood against a wall: it was smooth and fine on 3 sides, while the 4th side, which probably stood against the wall in the church, was not quite as finely finished. Shallow lengthwise grooves had been cut into the post.
blocks.21: I had the piece of post dated at the Radiological Dating Laboratory in Trondheim. Professor Reidar Nydal arranged the analysis of the material, and the dating report, dated 14 January 1994 and signed by Nydal and Fred H. Skogseth, shows that the material is most probably from 1455–1635 AD, that is, 359–539 years old.
blocks.22: As to the size and design of the church, an inspection in 1686 noted that the nave was 28 ells long and the chancel 10 ells. Nothing is said about the width. Nor is it written what type of church it was, other than that it was a log church with a porch, “as well as a modest tower”, and an “extension on the south side of the chancel”. The church was then roofed with tiles. It is said that two new windows were to be put in behind the altar and that the two “paintings” behind the altar were to be hung on “the north side of either the chancel or the nave”. The tower was to be clad with boards.
blocks.23: In 1668 the church got a new pulpit “decorated with carving”. In 1686 a new porch and “4 ells of canvas put on the tower's vane”. In 1694 “the old gallery above the women's pews was taken down and moved further down the church”. In 1697 19 turned columns were put between the chancel and the nave, “with a frame round them”. In 1700 the old altarpiece was restored and “furnished with new ironwork and with carving in limewood.” The joinery was done by a man much used “in these parts”, “Simen the Joiner”. I cannot find out who did “the carving”, but the name “Fredrich Wessel” is attached to it with the addition: “who probably ordered it”.
blocks.24: In 1703 a new transept was added on the north side of the church, and in 1706 “the gallery was moved into the new transept.” In 1712 new tiles were laid on the church and “the font was moved”. This was not the baptismal font we know, which at that time stood outside the churchyard gate, “beside the great cross.” In 1718 new turned “balusters” were put up over the chancel door and “a new font with a cover” was made.
blocks.25: In 1722 the church is described as a “handsome timber building”. On the north side half a transept had been added. There was a porch of staves in front of the main entrance and a smaller porch in front of the chancel door on the south side. The church was roofed with tiles throughout and well kept both “inside and out”. The chancel was given as “10 ells square”, the nave 27 ells long and 14 ells wide, the transept 12 ells long and 11 wide, the west porch “6 ells each side” and the south porch “4 ells long, 3 ells wide.”
blocks.26: From an inventory of the church's contents in 1690 it is very interesting to see that there was one of Christian III's Bibles here. Øverland's history of Norway says that only 96 copies of these Bibles came to Norway. The inventory mentions that the church is well supplied with books. There were thus two more Bibles, one of Frederick II's and one of Christian IV's. There were also 3 bells; one was quite small, and the middle one was cracked and lay down in the church. In 1712 two old “broken” bells were recast into one. In 1720 “a painted wooden box for the wafers” was bought.
blocks.27: According to “Dahl's account”, there was in 1811 an old altarpiece in the church that had been taken down in 1768 by the parish priest Sommer when he had a new one painted. There were also “2 old portraits of an unknown man and woman, painted in 1643”.
blocks.28: In the book by E. Bjordø mentioned earlier, he says that his grandfather told of a model of a sailing ship, a full-rigger, that hung from the church ceiling. When the church doors were opened, the sails fluttered and the ship swung gently on the ropes it hung from.
blocks.29: I have found nothing about what became of the old altarpiece and the pictures Dahl mentions, or the sailing ship Bjordø mentions in his book.
blocks.30: From about 1720 onwards many churches were sold at public auction, probably to raise money for the kings' wars. The church here was sold on 15 November 1723 to Magister Nicolai Stabel for “129 rix-dollars crowns”. Stabel was the priest here at the time. Three of the church's farms, Lid, Knarvik and Grimstad, were included in the sale. The royal deed is dated 12 August 1724. The church changed hands several times, and maintenance gradually failed; among other things the roof began to leak. With its 350 seats the church also became too small, as several of the priests pointed out in their reports to the bishop. Efforts were made to get a new church; Dahl in particular pressed hard for a new building in his time. The last owner of the church before it was sold back to “Eivindvig congregation” was the parish priest Daae in Fana. His widow, Edvardine Daae, signed the deed on 22 October 1862. This church was pulled down and sold at auction on 15 June 1863 at “the request of Eivindvig municipal council”. The auction was run by R. Haugland, with Lasse J. Sande and Mikkel Rørtveit as witnesses. There were 480 lots, which raised a total of 298 speciedaler and 19 shillings, and the remains of the church were scattered around the parish
blocks.32: A new law of 24 September 1851 had rules about how large a church should be in relation to the population of the parish. This law set off church building around the country. Another thing that probably also hastened the building of a new church
blocks.33: in our parish was that Dahl died on 4 August 1852. People held him in great esteem, and they wanted to honour his memory by building a new church, as he had worked so actively for.
blocks.34: The church question was dealt with by the municipal council twice in 1851 and became a frequent and topical item at council meetings in the years that followed. It became a large, difficult and costly matter. The old church had to be disposed of, the new one had to be financed and permits had to be obtained – there were many bodies the matter had to pass through.
blocks.35: The rules in the law of 24 September 1851 called for a church of just over 800 seats for our parish. The parish priest Meyer had pointed this out in his reports. The municipal council applied to build for 700 seats. They further applied for the municipality to “receive, without cost to itself, drawings and estimates prepared at this ministry's instigation”. It goes on to say that both the parish priest and the dean have “declared that a church fitted out for 700 seats will in any case be fully sufficient for the church-going common people.” By royal decree of 22 December 1860 permission was given to build the church with 700 seats. The cost of drawings and estimates was also covered. It says that “under the law of 25 February 1860 it is most graciously permitted that a new church designed for 700 seats be built in the main parish of Eivindvig”, and further: “..the ministry has, at public expense, had the building inspector prepare the enclosed drawings and estimates for a church of the size laid down in the decree.”
blocks.36: At meetings in Fonnevik on 1 April and 14 June 1862 the municipal council approved the drawings with small changes. The priest was instructed to find out where timber could be obtained most cheaply. Trygve and Kåre Lie have told, from their grandfather Truls Lie, that to keep the cost as low as possible, timber from Masfjorden was transported by binding it together into rafts, putting sails on the rafts and sailing it here that way. Truls was 6 years old when the church was built, and he remembered these “vessels” coming north through Brandangersundet.
blocks.37: The groundwork was to be done as voluntary communal work, with work teams of 6 men a day. “Those who do not attend must pay 36 shillings a day per man, 2 days per farmer and 1 day per crofter.”
blocks.38: Alf Sæternes says, from his father Anders Sæternes, that it was Lars i Livra who did the blasting of stone for the foundations. Lars said that the priest asked him not to blast so early in the morning. The priest did not want to be disturbed at the crack of dawn. But the very next morning Lars set off three blasts as soon as he arrived for work.
blocks.39: From what I have heard, it was Jon Midthun (farm no. 19, holding no. 1) who built the stone foundations under the church.
blocks.40: The church was built by the master builder Ole Syslak from Lindås, who took on the work for 5,560 speciedaler.
blocks.41: The new church was built on the same site where the old church stood. It became a beautiful long church. The nave is 19.9 m long and 12.6 m wide inside. The chancel is 5 sides of an octagon and measures 7.8 x 7.6 m. The church lies east–west. It was consecrated on the third Sunday of Advent, 13 December 1863. It was a great day of celebration for the people of the district. Even though the weather was not of the best, the church was full. The dean of Ytre Sogn deanery, Tommas Eriksen, performed the consecration, the parish priest Arnold Meyer officiated and several other members of the clergy were present. A man from the outer part of the parish who took part in the consecration himself has told: “For a long time there was doubt whether the church would be finished that year. I took part in the voluntary work with many others, mostly clearing up. We sailed home on Saturday evening. On Sunday it was grey and blowing fresh. But such a sight one would seldom see: the waterway was swarming with sails. In Prestesundet there was boat after boat, from the outer and the inner parts. Could the church really hold them all? Yes, space was tight. I still seem to hear the roar of the mighty hymn singing. The whole thing was a great and unforgettable occasion.” (O.B., b. 1841, d. 1928).
blocks.43: Old interior with the old organ at the top right. Photo: Jørgen L. Midtun.
blocks.44: In 1897 (according to Bjordø's book) a pipe organ came to the church, the same one that is still there. The altarpiece is signed C. Brun; the year appears to be 1872. The painting shows Jesus in Gethsemane, with the angel holding the chalice and sleeping apostles in the background. The altarpiece was put up, in a beautifully made frame, in 1873. Bjordø states that the two church bells were transferred from the old church. One bell was made in Bergen in 1711 and recast in Stockholm in 1821; the other has no inscription. (It has been said that the bell without an inscription is from the 15th century, but could it be the one that came from the two bells in the old church that were melted together into one in 1712?) Since then I have seen a note from a meeting where the archaeologist Alf Tore Hommedal, who was present among others, said that the bell with no inscription may well be from the 14th century. It has a Gothic shape, and its basic shape at the bottom is like the bells that were cast at Sola in the 12th century.
blocks.45: The two chandeliers hanging in the nave were received in 1912 as a gift from King Haakon VII and Queen Maud (after a “begging letter” from Johan Klokeid). The chandelier over the gallery is probably the one Sr. Michel Normann gave to the old church in 1706. The pulpit and the altar reredos are beautiful work of great value. I have already told the story of the solid baptismal font.
blocks.46: In the handwritten paper of the Eivindvik youth society, “Fremad”, of 3 December 1899, it says that the stoves for the church had then arrived at the “steamer office” but had not yet been installed. This shows that the stoves in the church were replaced around the turn of the century. These are probably the stoves we see in the picture of the church interior around 1913 in the 125th anniversary publication. The picture shows the stovepipes going straight up inside the church and through the roof. On the south side the stove stood far forward in the church, on the north side further back. Marks on the floor still show where the stoves stood. The chimneys were built during the rebuilding for the 75th anniversary in 1938.
blocks.47: For the 75th anniversary in 1938 the church was restored and renovated. Inside it was rebuilt and panelled with plywood boards, the organ was turned 90 degrees and built in, and the gallery got a solid front railing. The rebuilding was done to designs by the architect Johan Lindstrøm, and the painting to designs by the state consultant Dominicus Erdmann.
blocks.48: From what I have been told, during the renovation in 1938 the exit door that used to be in the south wall of the nave was moved to the north wall. It is said that when the church was built (1863) this door was placed on the north side in the drawings, but because “a man in Fonnevika” wanted to see who went to church, the door was put in the south wall after all. The man could then keep an eye on both the main door and the side door.
blocks.49: The master carpenter for the woodwork in 1938 was Søren K. Lie. His regular crew were Trygve Lie, Konrad Lund, Bernt A. Lid, Kristoffer Lund and Reidar Norstein. In addition some worked for shorter periods. The painting was done by the master painter Ola A. Korsvold, with Erling Korsvold and Erling Ullebø as assistants.
blocks.50: The spire was repaired in 1956 and given a copper covering instead of lead.
blocks.51: A Gulen native living elsewhere gave money for stained glass in the two chancel windows. These pieces were installed for the centenary in 1963. For this anniversary floodlights were also installed for the altarpiece and the altar. A baptismal vestry was added on the south side of the church, which was a great benefit for those who carried children to baptism. The priest's vestry was also put in order and renovated. Floodlights were also installed outside to light up the front and the tower. Our beautiful church looks fine in the floodlight, which was a gift from Gulen Kraftlag.
blocks.52: For the anniversary in 1963 some of the altar furnishings were also renewed. There were new candlesticks, some new altar silver, the baptismal bowl was restored and polished, a new water jug was bought, carpet was laid in the chancel and inside the altar rail, and there was new fabric on the pulpit and the altar table. Much of the new was given by Gulen natives living elsewhere.
blocks.53: Over the years people from the village living elsewhere have also given many other beautiful gifts to the church, among them the fine altar cloth and the flower vases on the altar, a beautiful tapestry for the carpet inside the altar rail, covers for the kneeler, four chasubles (one white, one green, one purple and one red), a silver chalice, paten and wafer box, etc.
blocks.54: In the years just before the centenary, electricity was installed in the church and the organ got an electric motor. Until then the large organ bellows had been driven by a hand pump. On feast days with many people in church, long hymns and loud music, the “bellows treader”, usually a young lad, could sometimes break into a sweat. I have tried it myself.
blocks.55: In these years a loudspeaker system was also installed in the church, and water was laid on to the church and the graveyard. In 1982 the loudspeaker system was replaced with a new one, bought with collected funds. The same year the cladding on the west wall and the entrance was replaced and a new main door put in. The year before, 1981, there was a major repair of the tower. A good deal of the timber was replaced, the outer wall of the upper part of the tower was renewed, and a new slate roof was laid. The old spire, made of wrought iron, had rusted through. A new brass spire was made in the same shape and put up. The ball is from the old spire. The new spire, made by Bernt Stendal as voluntary work, was highly praised by experts.
blocks.56: The baptismal vestry extension and the major repairs in 1955, 1963, 1981 and 1982 were carried out by the carpenters Magnus Kvamsdal, Mons Haveland, Einar Hope, Leif Nyhammer, Olav Brosvik and Henrik E. Haveland.
blocks.57: In 1986 wall lamps were bought for the church. The same year a wheelchair entrance was built on the north side. A handrail was put up at the main entrance.
blocks.59: A mortuary chapel by the church had long been badly missed. In 1979 the plans were realised and we got a good, modern mortuary chapel built next to the churchyard wall north of the church. The building fits nicely into the terrain. It has a turf roof, and the wall facing the churchyard gate is of grey stone. The building contains a mortuary, a wheelchair-accessible toilet and a break room and office. It was designed by the municipal engineer Trygve Asbjørn Wergeland and built by the firm Anton Olsen A/S, Bergen. Part of the cost was met with collected funds.
blocks.60: To make room for the mortuary chapel where it stands, the memorial to those who fell in the Second World War had to be moved about 20 m to the north-west. This memorial was raised in 1947 and unveiled before a large crowd on 3 August by Major Skåtun. Marines stood as guard of honour. It was the 75th birthday of King Haakon VII, a fine and very warm Sunday. The king's jubilee was marked in the church during the service before the unveiling. There was then a collection for the memorial stone, which raised 700 kroner.
blocks.61: In 1985 the first woman parish priest in the diocese of Bjørgvin, Signe Sandberg, took up her post here in the parish. On Easter Sunday she held her first service in office in Gulen church.
blocks.62: A PLACE OF GATHERING AND CULTURE
blocks.63: For generations the people of the district have had the church as their gathering place. They have come here in sorrow and in joy; many memories are kept here. In the days when they rowed and sailed to services, there was often a race between the boat crews to be first at the church. On the last stretch they got extra strength from the full, rich ring of the church bells. People brought a change of clothes and dressed in their finest before going in to the service. Besides the service, banns and other public announcements were also made on preaching Sundays. In the old days the announcements outside the church were almost as important to people as the newspapers are to us today.
blocks.64: The churchgoers gathered at Borggarden after the services. They brought plenty of food with them, took their time, ate, talked with acquaintances and caught up on the news. It could be well into the day before they set off home. It is said that young lads were given “drill exercises” at Borggarden after the services.
blocks.65: Borggarden is the area where "Herresalen" and "Borgstova" stand. A borggard is an open courtyard between buildings or walls in a castle. I have not managed to find anyone today who has heard that a castle stood here, but several of us older people remember the remains of a wall in the area by "Borgstova", and several say they have heard that remains of house foundations were found in the area. Perhaps a castle in really ancient times gave the area its name? And was it here that the servants of the parsonage lived?
blocks.66: We know that the priests did many kinds of community-building work. Dahl, for example, among much else, taught the teachers and arranged vaccinations and other medical services. It is quite likely that the priests used the time after the services, with many people gathered, for some of this work. I also know that the bank cashier, and probably other officials too, were given errands that they had to see to at the church. “Bring to the first preaching Sunday...” the customer's errand would often begin.
blocks.67: The instructions for the church caretaker, adopted by the municipal council on 19 November 1900, show that things were a little different then from now; among other things they say: “The church is to be washed 3 times a year and swept every other Saturday.” “...see that Borgstuen is washed 12 times a year and swept every Saturday”. The pay was 100 kroner a year, paid quarterly, “and the right to mow the churchyard.”
blocks.68: All the gifts and all the unpaid effort in work and fund-raising are good proof that the people of Gulen love their church. We are also proud of our church – it is beautiful and solid, and it is finely situated. If it could speak, it would surely have much to tell of priests, parish clerks, church caretakers, organists, the common people, beautiful singing, mighty music and a rich, pulsing life through many generations. May our church be cherished and well looked after, and continue to be a gathering place – a cultural centre – for the people.
blocks.70: A church anniversary in the old style at Prestekaia.
blocks.71: The church's 125th anniversary was celebrated on 4 September 1988. Although the weather was bad that Sunday, the grand celebration, a church festival in the old manner, went off well. Many wore costumes from “the old days” and came sailing and walking long distances to church; indeed some came in an old-fashioned horse-drawn cart. There was a bride with a crown and a historical play with a wedding procession. A “parish priest” and a “sheriff”, with their wives, all in old-fashioned dress, were also part of it.
blocks.72: The anniversary service was led by Dean Geir Sørebø, the parish priest Signe Sandberg and the former parish priest in Gulen, Olav Rossabø. Håkon Randal, a member of the Storting and a Gulen native living elsewhere, gave the festive address. Per Indrehus from Voss had composed and arranged a musical work with religious themes, which was premiered by a mixed choir of singers from Brekke male voice choir, Dalsøyra choir, Gulen church singing group and a children's choir from Dalsøyra school. The soloists were Berit Opheim, soprano, Olav Dale, saxophone and flute, Einar Mjølsnes, Hardanger fiddle, and Per Indrehus, synthesizer; the conductor was Ludvik Kjellevold. A mighty performance, which was recorded for later release on cassette.
blocks.73: In all there were probably 1,200 people present. It is said that about 1,000 people were inside the church during the service. Despite the bad weather this became a memorable church festival – a grand and fine anniversary.
blocks.75: The new organ at the back of the church. Photo: Henrik Tveit.
blocks.76: On Sunday 21 January 1996 a new pipe organ was consecrated by Dean Geir Sørebø during the service in the church. Bjørn Magne Hansen read the lessons and the parish priest Berit Bjørnerud preached. The church was almost full, and there was great joy that we had finally got a new organ after many years of procedure and fund-raising.
blocks.77: After the service there was a festive gathering at Eivindvik Hotel, with the ceremonial handing over of the organ key from the organ builder, Brødrene Torkildsen of Åsen in Nord-Trøndelag, represented by Per Øyvind Torkildsen, to the municipality, represented by the mayor Ola Byrknes, and on to the parish council, represented by its chair Helga Westervik.
blocks.78: The mayor presented a municipal coat of arms to Torkildsen and thanked him for work well done. Another who received great thanks and praise for his work was Jann-Magnar Fiskvik, who was responsible for the fine tonal result.
blocks.79: The dinner ended with coffee and “organ cake”. The cake, made by Ingrid H. Haveland and Eldbjørg Rutledal, was nicely shaped as a copy of the organ and tasted excellent.
blocks.80: After dinner we had the first concert on the new organ, by the consultant Stein Johannes Kolnes. “It was full-toned and fine, and shows beyond doubt that Gulen church has got an instrument to delight and inspire us and generations to come.” (Quoted from Gulen parish magazine no. 1 for 1996.)
blocks.81: The organ has 18 stops and 1,086 pipes. It cost NOK 1,789,367 including VAT. Collected funds, plus interest on the funds held in an account at the local bank, amounted to NOK 1,310,000; the municipality provided the rest.
blocks.82: The interior of the church looking towards the new organ. Magnor Midtun on the left guiding his relative, the conservationist Magne Midttun.
